$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sin}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sin}^{2}\,\theta \text{ }\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{({sin}^{3}\,\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sin}^{2}\,\theta \text{ }\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{6}\,\theta +9{sin}^{4}\,\theta \text{ }\,{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}\,\theta \sqrt{{sin}^{2}\,\theta +9{cos}^{2}\,\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}\,\theta \sqrt{1+8{cos}^{2}\,\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce35695c-d7ed-5650-b6f0-c0d7e8432851"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3}).

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{20-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}

over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{[|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})|-|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})|) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f262cbb1-b41b-5a16-a002-abeb999c9afc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)] \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f" :answer-field/id #uuid "20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3155478e-1b5a-5e18-bd4c-26ed84959b1d" "answer-abcd435e-c198-5b6e-9039-b510adba1e54" "answer-8234212b-ceff-57f4-a7ce-844e2d396499" "answer-9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" "answer-94931a58-c0c8-5c1d-bfbb-07691dddb8fc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3155478e-1b5a-5e18-bd4c-26ed84959b1d" :answer/id #uuid "3155478e-1b5a-5e18-bd4c-26ed84959b1d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-abcd435e-c198-5b6e-9039-b510adba1e54" :answer/id #uuid "abcd435e-c198-5b6e-9039-b510adba1e54" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8234212b-ceff-57f4-a7ce-844e2d396499" :answer/id #uuid "8234212b-ceff-57f4-a7ce-844e2d396499" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" :answer/id #uuid "9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94931a58-c0c8-5c1d-bfbb-07691dddb8fc" :answer/id #uuid "94931a58-c0c8-5c1d-bfbb-07691dddb8fc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
L = \displaystyle\int_C \, \textrm{d}s
$$

Now, if $C$ is defined parametrically as 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle, \quad a\leq t \leq b ,
$$

then we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as

$$
L = \int_{a}^{b}||\mathbf r'(t)||\,\textrm d t = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

Geometrically, we can think of $\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to a vanishingly small change in $t.$ By summing (integrating) all of these small changes, we arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173203 :tutorial/content "Let's now build up a geometric understanding of what the arc length element $\textrm d s$ means. First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle.
$$

Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)

According to the diagram we have

$$
\Delta x = x(t+\Delta t) - x(t), \qquad \Delta y = y(t+\Delta t) - y(t),
$$

where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as

$$
\Delta x \approx \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta y \approx \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\Delta t.
$$

The change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\  & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\  & =[{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s

\approx

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \Delta t.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta t \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \textrm d t
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173204 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the formula for the arc length element $\textrm d s$ for a curve defined using plane polar coordinates. We will use a similar geometric approach.

Consider a curve $r= r(\theta)$ defined using polar coordinates. Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/7f/7fa77b8d4ad159967f917b438096f472cbd7f541495847e11b919a6843e6259b.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta \theta$ in the parameter $\theta.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/10/105112a2bb993a13282c5f36190ca99a46d80a22a4203f653f7f67060e486d48.png)

From here, we see that the vector $\Delta \mathbf r$ can be approximated as the vector addition of two components:

- a vector of length $\Delta r$ acting parallel to $\mathbf r,$ and

- a vector of length $r\Delta \theta$ acting perpendicular to $\mathbf r.$

![](images/08/080fa1112410328ba369e1c2e5d70fc2e5ddba97606a2fdeaa90d61e3e20d874.png)

Note that $\Delta r$ is simply the difference of the radial lengths between the points $P$ and $P'.$ The expression $r\Delta \theta$ comes from the formula for the arc length of a sector of a circle.

Now, the change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Since our two components are perpendicular, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ≈(Δr)^{2}+(rΔ\theta )^{2} \\  & =Δ{r}^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, we have

$$
\Delta r = r(\theta + \Delta\theta) - r(\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\Delta\theta.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $(\Delta s)^2$ above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & ={r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & =[{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}](Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\Delta\theta.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta \theta \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\textrm d\theta
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172176 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

}{3})\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 3\pi $ ?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

Since $r=2{cos}^{3}⁡(\frac{\theta }{3})\,$ we have

"![](images/19/19725cfd8068973c899fcb4f54abcebbbfcd24bd68aec510b9d41cee2c2cd02a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{20-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1cca78f2-2d1d-5264-9180-c7409ad32bd4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{[|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})|-|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})|) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4d754845-5d58-59c1-864c-f3740c76cc59"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4d754845-5d58-59c1-864c-f3740c76cc59" :answer-field/id #uuid "4d754845-5d58-59c1-864c-f3740c76cc59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-59a4d601-d2b3-5c64-9a6e-78d2d155f615" :answer-field/choices ["answer-acf332da-f102-5954-a0ff-4632294d19b6" "answer-48d38326-3827-5037-8c94-f55b16de2521" "answer-59a4d601-d2b3-5c64-9a6e-78d2d155f615" "answer-2b8f5946-803e-549c-a59d-30354b99ca23" "answer-5272c95e-f96d-52e0-9de8-9b6c1893b269"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-acf332da-f102-5954-a0ff-4632294d19b6" :answer/id #uuid "acf332da-f102-5954-a0ff-4632294d19b6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48d38326-3827-5037-8c94-f55b16de2521" :answer/id #uuid "48d38326-3827-5037-8c94-f55b16de2521" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2+\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-59a4d601-d2b3-5c64-9a6e-78d2d155f615" :answer/id #uuid "59a4d601-d2b3-5c64-9a6e-78d2d155f615" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2b8f5946-803e-549c-a59d-30354b99ca23" :answer/id #uuid "2b8f5946-803e-549c-a59d-30354b99ca23" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4-\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5272c95e-f96d-52e0-9de8-9b6c1893b269" :answer/id #uuid "5272c95e-f96d-52e0-9de8-9b6c1893b269" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/id #uuid "6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-123581" :question/problem "![](images/36/36008a9155a01a07136cee263ce0a89239719227541536e8c2f8ea358d43e6df.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f262cbb1-b41b-5a16-a002-abeb999c9afc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)] \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f" :answer-field/id #uuid "20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3155478e-1b5a-5e18-bd4c-26ed84959b1d" "answer-abcd435e-c198-5b6e-9039-b510adba1e54" "answer-8234212b-ceff-57f4-a7ce-844e2d396499" "answer-9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" "answer-94931a58-c0c8-5c1d-bfbb-07691dddb8fc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3155478e-1b5a-5e18-bd4c-26ed84959b1d" :answer/id #uuid "3155478e-1b5a-5e18-bd4c-26ed84959b1d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-abcd435e-c198-5b6e-9039-b510adba1e54" :answer/id #uuid "abcd435e-c198-5b6e-9039-b510adba1e54" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8234212b-ceff-57f4-a7ce-844e2d396499" :answer/id #uuid "8234212b-ceff-57f4-a7ce-844e2d396499" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" :answer/id #uuid "9eeb0c86-cf6c-5ccc-baf9-def02136f813" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94931a58-c0c8-5c1d-bfbb-07691dddb8fc" :answer/id #uuid "94931a58-c0c8-5c1d-bfbb-07691dddb8fc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
L = \displaystyle\int_C \, \textrm{d}s
$$

Now, if $C$ is defined parametrically as 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle, \quad a\leq t \leq b ,
$$

then we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as

$$
L = \int_{a}^{b}||\mathbf r'(t)||\,\textrm d t = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

Geometrically, we can think of $\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to a vanishingly small change in $t.$ By summing (integrating) all of these small changes, we arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173203 :tutorial/content "Let's now build up a geometric understanding of what the arc length element $\textrm d s$ means. First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle.
$$

Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)

According to the diagram we have

$$
\Delta x = x(t+\Delta t) - x(t), \qquad \Delta y = y(t+\Delta t) - y(t),
$$

where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as

$$
\Delta x \approx \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta y \approx \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\Delta t.
$$

The change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\  & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\  & =[{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s

\approx

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \Delta t.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta t \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \textrm d t
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173204 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the formula for the arc length element $\textrm d s$ for a curve defined using plane polar coordinates. We will use a similar geometric approach.

Consider a curve $r= r(\theta)$ defined using polar coordinates. Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/7f/7fa77b8d4ad159967f917b438096f472cbd7f541495847e11b919a6843e6259b.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta \theta$ in the parameter $\theta.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/10/105112a2bb993a13282c5f36190ca99a46d80a22a4203f653f7f67060e486d48.png)

From here, we see that the vector $\Delta \mathbf r$ can be approximated as the vector addition of two components:

- a vector of length $\Delta r$ acting parallel to $\mathbf r,$ and

- a vector of length $r\Delta \theta$ acting perpendicular to $\mathbf r.$

![](images/08/080fa1112410328ba369e1c2e5d70fc2e5ddba97606a2fdeaa90d61e3e20d874.png)

Note that $\Delta r$ is simply the difference of the radial lengths between the points $P$ and $P'.$ The expression $r\Delta \theta$ comes from the formula for the arc length of a sector of a circle.

Now, the change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Since our two components are perpendicular, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ≈(Δr)^{2}+(rΔ\theta )^{2} \\  & =Δ{r}^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, we have

$$
\Delta r = r(\theta + \Delta\theta) - r(\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\Delta\theta.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $(\Delta s)^2$ above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & ={r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & =[{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}](Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\Delta\theta.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta \theta \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\textrm d\theta
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172176 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-7aa4e4d5-0080-5cb6-bebe-9d6c94950127" :question/id #uuid "7aa4e4d5-0080-5cb6-bebe-9d6c94950127"] ["question-7aa4e4d5-0080-5cb6-bebe-9d6c94950127" :question/math-academy-id "q-123511"] ["question-7aa4e4d5-0080-5cb6-bebe-9d6c94950127" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sin}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ ?"] ["question-7aa4e4d5-0080-5cb6-bebe-9d6c94950127" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={csc}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-3{csc}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({csc}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-3{csc}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{6}⁡\theta +9{csc}^{6}⁡\theta {cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{cot}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=3+\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?"] ["question-8c80223d-79b2-5d97-8d88-3fa6275a012a" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3+\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3+\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9+6\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9+6\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta +1+8{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10+6\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta +8{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8c80223d-79b2-5d97-8d88-3fa6275a012a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-970ad32f-3bc8-5eae-a83f-06f38e693fb2" :answer-field/id #uuid respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{3\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{e}^{3\theta }.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{3\theta })}^{2}+{(3{e}^{3\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{6\theta }+9{e}^{6\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{10{e}^{6\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}{e}^{3\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}({e}^{3\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}

is the path along the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi .$"] ["question-1b5a0004-da97-5a43-bf86-5bd3413d5383" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{[|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})|-|-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})|) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1b5a0004-da97-5a43-bf86-5bd3413d5383" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-4d754845-5d58-59c1-864c-f3740c76cc59" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-123581"] ["question-6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/problem Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above."] ["question-6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f262cbb1-b41b-5a16-a002-abeb999c9afc" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-27eda322-b707-5345-adf8-0465217fdeaf" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{2}⁡\theta (1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{sec}^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)] \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-27eda322-b707-5345-adf8-0465217fdeaf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-27eda322-b707-5345-adf8-0465217fdeaf" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-20dcdcfd-748c-52ae-895b-79a3d2f6200f"] [17592186172090 :knowledge-point/questions "question-27eda322-b707-5345-adf8-0465217fdeaf"] [17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
L = \displaystyle\int_C \, \textrm{d}s
$$

Now, if $C$ is defined parametrically as 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle, \quad a\leq t \leq b ,
$$

then we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as

$$
L = \int_{a}^{b}||\mathbf r'(t)||\,\textrm d t = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

Geometrically, we can think of $\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to a vanishingly small change in $t.$ By summing (integrating) all of these small changes, we arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson."] [17592186173203 :tutorial/content "Let's now build up a geometric understanding of what the arc length element $\textrm d s$ means. First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle.
$$

Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)

According to the diagram we have

$$
\Delta x = x(t+\Delta t) - x(t), \qquad \Delta y = y(t+\Delta t) - y(t),
$$

where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as

$$
\Delta x \approx \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta y \approx \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\Delta t.
$$

The change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get

$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1+\sin\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+4{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following identities:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})=1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting our integral using the above identities, we can evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =4\sqrt{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}((0+1)-(-1+0)) \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048717} {:db/id 17592186049303} {:db/id 17592186172287 :question/id #uuid "f2b06f7c-408a-5dfe-b281-0fde1f80e146" :question/math-academy-id "q-123354"} {:db/id 17592186172290 {:db/id 17592186172995 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$
L = \displaystyle\int_C \, \textrm{d}s
$$

Now, if $C$ is defined parametrically as 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle, \quad a\leq t \leq b ,
$$

then we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as

$$
L = \int_{a}^{b}||\mathbf r'(t)||\,\textrm d t = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t\,.
$$

Geometrically, we can think of $\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to a vanishingly small change in $t.$ By summing (integrating) all of these small changes, we arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson.

The idea of an arc length element is useful when we want to think about line integrals in different coordinate systems. It also illustrates a fundamental relationship between the arc length of a path and a line integral of a function along that path." :tutorial/id #uuid "56e8bdd3-5303-5eeb-82d3-ef837773c38f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5797 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "65361afd-5d8b-59a0-8bed-041764bc0685" :step/math-academy-id 35544 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172996}} {:db/id 17592186172996 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173202 :tutorial/content "Now suppose that a curve $C$ is defined using plane polar coordinates as

$$
r = r(\theta), \qquad \theta_1\leq\theta\leq\theta_2.
$$

We've already seen that a polar curve is just a special type of parametric curve in the parameter $\theta,$ where

$$
x = r(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y = r(\theta)\sin\theta, \qquad \theta_1\leq\theta\leq\theta_2.
$$

Using the usual formula for the arc length of a polar curve, the arc length of $C$ can be calculated as

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta
$$

which is the same as the line integral

$$
L = \displaystyle\int\limits_C \, \textrm{d}s.
$$

By comparing our two expressions for $L,$ the arc-length element $\textrm ds$ for a curve can also be defined using polar coordinates as follows:

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta
$$

We'll build up a geometric understanding of this result at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's use this result to calculate some line integrals across polar curves." :tutorial/id #uuid "4850750a-5b8d-5c03-88c1-a2b832a313ce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5801 :tutorial/title "The Arc Length Element for Polar Curves"} :step/id #uuid "665cda4d-3863-540c-afb3-a1cde7ebd6d9" :step/math-academy-id 35565 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172993}} {:db/id 17592186172997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173203 :tutorial/content "Let's now build up a geometric understanding of what the arc length element $\textrm d s$ means. First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle.
$$

Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)

According to the diagram we have

$$
\Delta x = x(t+\Delta t) - x(t), \qquad \Delta y = y(t+\Delta t) - y(t),
$$

where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as

$$
\Delta x \approx \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta y \approx \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\Delta t.
$$

The change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & \approx ||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\  & \approx {(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\  & =[{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s

\approx

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \Delta t.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta t \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \textrm d t
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65578a76-05f7-551a-acbd-956ae6831965" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5802 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "46feb8c2-5068-5992-a3a2-858b37d8c39e" :step/math-academy-id 35569 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172998}} {:db/id 17592186172998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173204 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the formula for the arc length element $\textrm d s$ for a curve defined using plane polar coordinates. We will use a similar geometric approach.

Consider a curve $r= r(\theta)$ defined using polar coordinates. Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/7f/7fa77b8d4ad159967f917b438096f472cbd7f541495847e11b919a6843e6259b.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta \theta$ in the parameter $\theta.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/10/105112a2bb993a13282c5f36190ca99a46d80a22a4203f653f7f67060e486d48.png)

From here, we see that the vector $\Delta \mathbf r$ can be approximated as the vector addition of two components:

- a vector of length $\Delta r$ acting parallel to $\mathbf r,$ and

- a vector of length $r\Delta \theta$ acting perpendicular to $\mathbf r.$

![](images/08/080fa1112410328ba369e1c2e5d70fc2e5ddba97606a2fdeaa90d61e3e20d874.png)

Note that $\Delta r$ is simply the difference of the radial lengths between the points $P$ and $P'.$ The expression $r\Delta \theta$ comes from the formula for the arc length of a sector of a circle.

Now, the change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Since our two components are perpendicular, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & \approx ||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & \approx (Δr)^{2}+(rΔ\theta )^{2} \\  & =Δ{r}^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, we have

$$
\Delta r = r(\theta + \Delta\theta) - r(\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\Delta\theta.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $(\Delta s)^2$ above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & \approx {(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & ={r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & =[{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}](Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\Delta\theta.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta \theta \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\textrm d\theta
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b310dc84-9da7-5492-9639-145086fe7403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5803 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Polar Curve"} :step/id #uuid "6cd1a226-a48b-5c1c-9eed-9c80bd2de431" :step/math-academy-id 35570}] :activity/title "Further Properties of Line Integrals of Scalar Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172176} {:db/id 17592186172995 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\mathbin{:}$

$$

First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle.
$$

Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)

According to the diagram we have

$$
\Delta x = x(t+\Delta t) - x(t), \qquad \Delta y = y(t+\Delta t) - y(t),
$$

where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as

$$
\Delta x \approx \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta y \approx \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\Delta t.
$$

The change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & \approx ||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\  & \approx {(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\  & =[{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s

\approx

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \Delta t.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta t \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \textrm d t
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65578a76-05f7-551a-acbd-956ae6831965" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5802 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Parametric Curve"} {:db/id 17592186172998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173204 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the formula for the arc length element $\textrm d s$ for a curve defined using plane polar coordinates. ![](images/10/105112a2bb993a13282c5f36190ca99a46d80a22a4203f653f7f67060e486d48.png)

$$
\textrm d s

17592186045417] [17592186046660 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in [17592186171895 1069 "e-9492" 17592186045417] [17592186171895 1071 "![](images/cd/cd1ba2536264e122c84377a1892c3ca86dd8f273b2eab9ba0e2c53eeb504ef65.png)

  

Find a definite integral with respect to $\theta$ that's equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-\sin{\theta}\,$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq  \pi,$ shown above." 17592186045417] [17592186171895 1072 #uuid "f6f11512-c37f-5922-b642-5290003b1d91" 17592186045417] [17592186171895 1074 "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=1-\sin{\theta},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = -\cos{\theta}.
$$
